newsitem.title: POLAND: Foreign countries rush aid to flooded Poland.
newsitem.headline: Foreign countries rush aid to flooded Poland.

text.p: Poland on Friday warmly thanked some 30 countries which have rushed more than $10 million in funds, equipment and other aid to help its battle against floods ravaging the south and west.

"The scale of humanitarian aid which Poland has had from some tens of countries and from international organisations exceeds $10 million," Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati told a news conference, stressing the speed of the response.

He said this grant aid was an immediate response to the emergency and larger sums were expected from the European Union via the United Nations and in preferential credits from the World Bank to help reconstruction of devastated areas.
Rosati singled out countries which had sent much-needed teams of rescuers or experts -- Sweden, Denmark, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Ukraine, Lithuania and Hungary.
"I would like to give very warm thanks for this help," he said.
International officials said the scale of the aid was considerable by standards in such disasters worldwide.
Rosati singled out the government of the small neighbouring former Soviet republic of Lithuania, which has offered $125,000. "This is very friendly, and very moving," he said.

This was more than the $100,000 announced by U.S. President Bill Clinton who visited Poland on July 10 as the disaster began, but Rosati said this sum was merely the maximum Clinton could offer without a decision by Congress.
A team of U.S. experts was arriving on Friday, said Rosati, who declined to speculate what else Washington may offer.

Much help, including vital heavy-duty water pumps, has come from the large Polish-American community, while the U.S. aid agency USAID has diverted funds from other projects in Poland for flood-related purposes.
Polish officials said they did not have full data on what foreign aid had been offered or supplied as donors sometimes did not notify central authorities.
A partial list of donors, compiled by Polish authorities, included Germany which has also been afflicted by the floods.
Germany offered help of 9.4 million zlotys ($2.7 million) that included 67 rescue workers active in each of the afflicted southwest Poland cities of Wroclaw and Opole.
Among bigger donors were the governments of Norway with 1.3 million zlotys and Hungary offering 4.38 million zlotys for water pumps, telecommunications equipment, medicines and food.

Britain had offered 100,000 pounds sterling ($167,000) for medical equipment, which was being channelled through the United Nations. The U.N. Warsaw envoy said more such contributions were expected to roll in.
The European Commission was due to authorise shifting 65 million Ecus earlier earmarked for other programmes in Poland for flood relief and reconstruction.
This, along with a $300 million soft loan expected from the World Bank, will contribute to rebuilding in affected areas, made especially urgent by the approach of winter four months away.
